title: Comparatives and Superlatives
summary: Two things or three? Comparative vs superlative, no double forms, irregular words, fewer/less, between/among, as … as and logical comparisons — taught for the ACT with worked items and a 10-question quiz.

blocks.text: Comparison errors are small — one word, sometimes one ending — but they appear in many ACT essays because writers compare things all the time: two products, three cities, last year and this year. This lesson covers every comparison rule the test uses: comparative vs superlative, double comparisons, irregular forms, fewer vs less, between vs among, *as … as*, and the subtle ones — comparing like with like and *than any other*.
What this question type tests

Comparison questions are usage questions in **Conventions of Standard English**, which is **38–43%** of the 40 scored ACT English questions (together with punctuation and sentence structure). The format is the usual one: an underlined portion, four choices, usually **NO CHANGE** first. A vertical scan of the choices tells you the type: larger / largest / more large / more larger, fewer / less, between / among, as / than.
Your method: **count the things being compared** and **check what kind of noun follows**. Most comparison items are solved by those two checks.
Rule 1: Two things → comparative; three or more → superlative

rows: Of the two routes, the coastal road is **shorter**.
It is the **shortest** of the three routes.
Karim is **the taller** of the twins.
one thing vs all the rest
Aswan has the **hottest** summer of any city we visited.

blocks.text: **Which ending?** One-syllable adjectives take -er/-est (tall, taller, tallest). Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change y to i (busy, busier, busiest; easy, easier). Most other adjectives of two or more syllables use more/most (more careful, most expensive). Adverbs ending in -ly use more/most (more quickly, most carefully).

rows: Of the two candidates, Mona is the most qualified.
Of all the planets, Jupiter is the larger.
Between tea and coffee, I like tea best.
This exam was difficulter than the last one.
She finished quicklier than her brother.

blocks.text: Rule 2: Never double a comparison
Use **either** the ending **or** the word more/most — never both, and never more/most with an irregular form.

items: ✗ more better → ✓ better
✗ most fastest → ✓ fastest
✗ more easier → ✓ easier
✗ more worse → ✓ worse
✗ the most best → ✓ the best

**Absolute adjectives** (unique, perfect, complete, equal) describe something that cannot have degrees in careful writing. ✗ The design is very unique / more unique. ✓ The design is **unique**. If a choice adds *more* or *very* to such a word and another choice is plain, the plain one is safer on the ACT.

blocks.text: Rule 3: Learn the irregular forms

**farther vs further — the memory trick:** far**ther** contains *far*, so use it for real **distance** you could measure. **Further** means *more / additional / to a greater degree*: "After **further** discussion, the plan was approved." ✗ "After farther discussion." When the sentence is about distance, the ACT treats *farther* as the safe answer.

blocks.title: اتنين ولا أكتر؟
blocks.text: عد الحاجات اللي بتتقارن. لو اتنين: er أو more (better, larger). لو تلاتة أو أكتر: est أو most (best, largest). وماتجمعش الاتنين أبدًا: more better غلط. وخلي بالك من الشاذ: good–better–best و bad–worse–worst.
Rule 4: fewer vs less, many vs much, number vs amount
Ask: **can I count it?** If you can put a number in front of the noun (three cars, ten mistakes), it is countable. If not (water, traffic, time, information), it is uncountable.

rows: **less** than twenty litres (one amount — see the note below)

items: ✗ The new road has less accidents. → ✓ The new road has **fewer** accidents.
✗ We had fewer rain this year. → ✓ We had **less** rain this year.
✗ a large amount of tourists → ✓ a large **number** of tourists

**Subtle case:** numbers that describe a single amount of time, money, distance or weight take *less*: ✓ The trip took **less than two hours**. ✓ It costs **less than fifty pounds**. You are thinking of one amount of time or money, not separate hours or pounds.
**Quick check:** if you could say *fewer* + a plural noun you can count one by one, do it: fewer items, fewer calories, fewer errors.

blocks.text: Rule 5: between vs among

items: **between** = two people or things: ✓ The prize was shared **between** the two finalists. ✓ **between** you and me
**among** = three or more, as a group: ✓ The work was divided **among** the five volunteers. ✓ a favourite **among** students
✗ The tension between the members of the large committee grew. → ✓ **among** the members (a group of many)
✗ Choose between the four options. → ✓ Choose **among** the four options. (ACT rule: two → between, three or more → among.)

blocks.text: Rule 6: as … as, so … that, and the …, the …

rows: The new phone is **as** light **as** the old one.
as light than the old one
faster then the bus / faster as the bus
**The more** you read, **the better** you write.
The more you read, better you write.
The road was **so** narrow **that** buses could not pass.
so narrow as buses could not pass
as many tickets as · as much effort as

blocks.text: **Do not mix the two shapes.** *as … as* is for equal things; *-er/more … than* is for unequal things. A choice like "as large or larger than" is incomplete; the full form is "as large **as** or larger **than**" — the ACT will usually offer a simpler correct choice instead.
Rule 7: Compare like with like

A comparison must be **logical**: you can compare a population with a population, not a population with a city. This is the hardest comparison item on the ACT because the wrong version sounds perfectly natural.

rows: Cairo's population is larger than Alexandria.
Cairo's population is larger than **Alexandria's** / than **that of** Alexandria.
The prices at the new shop are lower than the old shop.
Her essay was longer than her classmates.
Her essay was longer than **her classmates' essays** / **those of** her classmates.
Like other students, my grades improved.
Like other students, **I** improved my grades.

blocks.text: **Use *that of* for a singular noun and *those of* for a plural noun.** The climate of Aswan is drier than **that of** Cairo (that = the climate). The streets of Zamalek are quieter than **those of** downtown (those = the streets).
Rule 8: than any other
When you compare one member of a group with the rest of the group, add **other** or **else**, or the thing is compared with itself.

items: ✗ The Nile is longer than any river in Africa. (The Nile is a river in Africa, so it would be longer than itself.) → ✓ longer than **any other** river in Africa.
✗ Ahmed scored higher than anyone in his class. → ✓ higher than **anyone else** in his class.
✓ The Nile is longer than **any** river in Europe. (No *other* needed: the Nile is not in Europe.)

blocks.title: قارن حاجة بحاجة من نفس النوع
blocks.text: ماينفعش تقارن population بمدينة. قول Cairo's population is larger than that of Alexandria. استخدم that of للمفرد و those of للجمع. ولو بتقارن حاجة بباقي مجموعتها قول any other. وكمان: fewer مع الحاجات اللي بتتعد (fewer cars) و less مع اللي مابتتعدش (less water)، و between لاتنين و among لتلاتة أو أكتر.
Worked examples
Each example is a sentence from an ACT-style essay. The underlined portion is shown in **bold**.
**Worked example 1 — two vs three.** "Our team tested three types of solar panel, and the thin black model produced the **more electricity**."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) most electricity
C) mostest electricity
D) more electricity than

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** Three panels are compared, so the superlative **most** is needed.
**A** is the comparative, used only for two. **Trap:** the comparative sounds acceptable because the sentence does not repeat the number three.
**C** is not an English word.
**D** begins a comparison (*than*) but never finishes it.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — fewer vs less.** "Since the city added bus lanes, commuters have reported **less delays** on their way to work."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) fewer delays
C) lesser delays
D) a smaller amount of delays

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** *Delays* can be counted (one delay, two delays), so use **fewer**.
**A** uses *less*, which is for uncountable nouns (less traffic).
**C** *lesser* means *smaller in importance* (a lesser problem), not a smaller number.
**D** *amount* is also for uncountable nouns; it should be *number*, and the phrase is wordy anyway.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — illogical comparison.** "Researchers found that the memory of older elephants is more reliable than **younger elephants**."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) younger elephants are
C) that of younger elephants
D) those of younger elephants

blocks.text: **Answer: C.**

items: **C is correct.** The sentence compares *the memory* of older elephants with *the memory* of younger ones. *That of* (singular, = the memory of) keeps the comparison logical.
**A** compares a memory with elephants. **Trap:** illogical comparison; it sounds natural.
**B** still compares a memory with elephants and adds a verb.
**D** uses the plural *those*, but *memory* is singular. **Trap:** right idea, wrong number.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — than any other.** "In its first year, the town's new library attracted more visitors than **any project** the council had ever built."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) any other project
C) all projects
D) any projects

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** The library is itself one of the council's projects, so it must be compared with **any other** project.
**A** compares the library with itself. **Trap:** missing *other*.
**C** has the same logic problem (*all projects* includes the library).
**D** *any* + plural is awkward here and keeps the logic error.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5 — as … as.** "My grandmother insists that the new bakery's bread is not as soft **than** the bread she bought as a child."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) then
C) as
D) like

blocks.text: **Answer: C.**

items: **C is correct.** The structure is *not as* + adjective + **as**.
**A** mixes the *as … as* shape with the *-er than* shape.
**B** *then* is a time word, not a comparison word.
**D** *like* cannot complete the *as … as* structure.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Superlative for two:** "the best of the two", "the most qualified of the two" → better, more qualified.
**Double comparison:** more better, most fastest, more worse.
**Countable/uncountable:** less mistakes, an amount of people → fewer mistakes, a number of people.
**between for a group:** between the five members → among.
**Mixed shapes:** as … than, so … as → as … as, so … that.
**Illogical comparison:** Cairo's population vs Alexandria → that of Alexandria / Alexandria's.
**Missing *other*:** taller than any student in the class → any other student.
**farther/further:** farther = measurable distance; further = more, additional.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Count the things compared: two → -er/more; three or more → -est/most.
Eliminate every double form (more + -er, most + -est) immediately.
fewer/less, many/much, number/amount? Ask: can I count the noun?
between/among? Two → between; three or more → among.
See *than* or *as*? Check the shape (as … as / -er … than) and then check that the two things compared are the same kind of thing.
Comparing one member with its own group? Look for *other* or *else*.

blocks.text: Practice
Two short ACT-style essays with 5 questions each. The numbers in brackets match the question numbers. Every question tests comparisons.

blocks.title: Comparatives and Superlatives — ACT-style practice
blocks.intro: Two ACT-style essays, 10 questions. Choose the best version of each underlined portion; NO CHANGE keeps the original. Explanations appear after you answer.

questions.p:
Two Bicycles

Last summer I finally saved enough money to buy my first bicycle. The shop near our building had only two models in my price range, so I rode each one around the car park twice. The red one was lighter, but the blue one had __more better__ [1] brakes.

The salesman, a retired cyclist named Fathy, told me that the blue bike was the __strongest__ [2] of the two. He also pointed out that it would need __less__ [3] repairs, since its chain was sealed against the dust of Cairo's streets.

I chose the blue bike, and now I ride to school every morning, a trip of about four kilometres. On the first day I took a wrong turn and rode much __farther__ [4] than I needed to, but the next morning I found a shortcut along the canal. My cousin, who takes the bus, likes to tease me that a bicycle is not as fast __than__ [5] a bus. I don't mind. The ride is the best part of my day.
questions.q: [1] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: *Better* is already the comparative of *good*; adding *more* (A) is a double comparison. C is not standard; D is the superlative, but only two bikes are compared.

questions.e: "Of the two" means only two bikes are compared, so the comparative **stronger** is needed. A, B and C are all superlatives (for three or more), and B also uses *most* with a one-syllable adjective.

questions.e: *Repairs* is a countable plural noun, so it takes **fewer**. *Less* (A) is for uncountable nouns; *lesser* (B) means less important; *amount* (D) is also for uncountable nouns.

questions.p:
Our Snack Survey

For a science project, our class asked 120 students in our school which of three snacks they liked best: dates, popcorn or fruit salad. We expected one snack to win easily, but the votes were divided __between__ [6] the three snacks more evenly than anyone had predicted.

Popcorn received the __most__ [7] votes, with fruit salad close behind. Students who chose dates said that they ate them more often than __any snack__ [8], usually with breakfast. We also compared prices in the school shop and found that the price of fruit salad was higher than __popcorn__ [9].

Our teacher told us that a survey becomes more useful as it grows. Indeed, the more students we interviewed, __more interesting__ [10] the results became. Next term we plan to repeat the survey with every class in the school.
questions.q: [6] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: Three snacks are involved, so use **among** (three or more). *Between* (A, B) is for two; D is not standard English.

questions.e: Dates are one of the snacks, so they must be compared with **any other snack**; otherwise dates are compared with themselves. C and D keep the logic problem and are awkward.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Two → -er/more; three or more → -est/most; never both (no *more better*).
Irregular: good/well–better–best, bad/badly–worse–worst, far–farther (distance)/further (more).
fewer + countable, less + uncountable; between two, among three or more.
as … as for equal; -er … than for unequal; the more …, the more ….
Compare like with like (that of / those of) and use *any other* inside the same group.
